angle: A battlecruiser that verified itself into a combo deck: six checker-passed case files earned six pilot-approved swaps, moved the bracket floor from 3 to 4, and left one honest tension — every infinite routes through a single Aggravated Assault that five of the deck's own mana sources can never legally pay, so Treasures are the wallet.

teases: COMBATS 6 AND 12: one Gnawbone, one enchantment, two dead opponents — and the 22 Treasures you hold when the game ends
SIX SWAPS, SIX CASE FILES: the deck that upgraded itself through its own verification loop
REFUTED: Sneak Attack cannot cheat your commander — CR 903.6 says no, and we name the card that can
THE SPELLS-ONLY TRAP: five mana sources that can never pay the win

departments.note: The Ur-Dragon at hero scale from the pilot's printing — art by Jaime Jones (this issue's Featured Artist; the credit line under the art sets up the department). Tagline 'Nine mana. Worth it.' from issue.json, verbatim. The dominant coverline names verified stack 006's ending: the second opponent dies on combat 12 and the game ends before the last Treasure trigger resolves. Both violators are true: six checker-passed case files, and a computed bracket floor of 4 that the pilot asked for in writing (pilot_feedback.md). Vol. 005, updated in place per the Heliod precedent — the issue documents the deck it now describes, sha edc6644d0683.

Two-bucket contents (THIS ISSUE'S DECK / EVERY ISSUE) plus the tier legend printed in full — Vol. 005 may be somebody's first. The Kill's promise line should read 'two infinites, two bursts, one inversion, one refutation — all six stamped'. Upgrade Watch's promise line flags the pivot up front: 'the swaps already happened — now we go shopping: ten ranked picks from the whole pool, zero promises.'

departments.headline: THE DECK THAT UPGRADED ITSELF
departments.dek: The table reads five-colour Dragons as a battlecruiser, and for four turns they're right. Then the verification loop's six swaps show up — and the deck they earned is a combo deck wearing a battlecruiser costume, built around a commander it almost never casts.

callouts.title: LOOK SLOW, RAMP FAST
callouts.text: Turns one through four you are a mana deck, and you want to look like one: rocks, Farseek, Nature's Lore, a modal 3-drop — ramp or fixing is in hand by turn 6 in 71.6% of games. A ramping Dragon deck reads as slow; keep it that way. Do not lead with Aggravated Assault. It is the deck's loudest tell, and it wins nothing from turn two.

callouts.title: WAVES UNDER WRATH MATH
callouts.text: Turns five through seven, deploy Dragons in waves, never all at once — except when Wrathful Red Dragon is out, when an opposing damage sweeper becomes a 39-point execution aimed at one face (case A-004). Sneak Attack and Hellkite Courser compress the clock: {R} cheats any Dragon in the 99 into combat (case A-005), and Courser rents the commander for one hasty, draw-heavy attack.

callouts.title: TAKE THE WINDOW ONCE
callouts.text: The pivot is concrete: Aggravated Assault live with a connecting Old Gnawbone or Savage Ventmaw — the verified table-kill and the verified self-funding loop (cases A-006, A-003). Protection is in hand by turn 6 in 66.0% of games; hold it for exactly that turn. Every earlier turn, stay boring and let the table watch a commander you were never in a hurry to cast.

captions.The Ur-Dragon: **THE DISCOUNT, NOT THE DRAGON:** Eminence takes {1} off every other Dragon spell from the command zone, all game, without him ever being cast — the engine you are guaranteed on turn zero.
captions.Aggravated Assault: **THE ACTUAL CLOCK:** all three of this deck's two-card infinites route through this one enchantment. It comes down the turn it wins — with funding already on the table — or it stays in hand.
captions.Korlessa, Scale Singer: **THE SECOND HAND:** a two-mana Dragon that casts Dragon spells off the top of your library — rigged by Path of Ancestry's scry and Herald's Horn's peek, compounded by the Eminence discount.

pilot_tips.text: Trade Atsushi, the Blazing Sky freely — his death mints three unrestricted Treasures, which is exactly the mana that legally pays Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R}.

departments.pull_quote: The table is watching a commander you were never in a hurry to cast.

departments.headline: EMINENCE DOMAIN
departments.dek: What is the command zone guarantee worth when the guaranteed card costs nine mana? Everything — because this commander's best ability works from the zone, which makes him the one commander in the format you should almost never cast.
departments.body: Start with the guarantee (CR 903.4): your commander is the only card you always have — and The Ur-Dragon inverts what that usually means, because Eminence is a static discount that applies while he sits in the command zone. You are not guaranteed a body; you are guaranteed a rules engine. The goldfish makes the inversion policy, not preference: mean cast turn 8.967, cast by turn 6 in exactly zero of 10,000 runs. The tax math (CR 903.8) seals it: first cast nine (seven with Urza's Incubator out — Eminence discounts every OTHER Dragon spell, never himself), second cast eleven, third thirteen. At those prices recasting is not a plan, it is a catastrophe, so protection beats speed by a mile (strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance) — and the deck's flagship insurance has a clause worth reading twice: Deflecting Swat is free only while you CONTROL a commander, and Eminence does not switch it on; until The Ur-Dragon or a Hellkite Courser loan puts him on the battlefield, you pay retail. Courser is the real cheat: his trigger loans the commander from the command zone, hasty, for one attack — draw per attacking Dragon, free permanent from hand — and 903.8 taxes casts from the command zone, which a loan never is; the commander goes home at end step untaxed. Color identity: five colours lock nothing out of the 99 — the cost lands entirely on the manabase, and deck-facts prices it exactly (red wants 36 sources by the pip math against 15 red lands; black 36 against 11; Treasures, rocks, and the five-colour lands carry the gap). The 21-damage clock (CR 903.10a) is real but it is a coincidence with a trap in the arithmetic: at 10 power, two clean connections deal 20 — one point short — so budget three connections, or one point of pump (a single Lathliss activation closes it). The political read: this commander is face-up information from turn zero, so the table prices in the ending before your first land. That is the one tax Eminence never discounts — and the Politics Table department is about paying it on your schedule, not theirs.

captions.Hellkite Courser: **THE LOAN OFFICER:** puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone, hasty, for one attack — the trigger without the nine mana, no tax ever accrues, and he goes home at end step.
captions.Deflecting Swat: **READ THE FREE CLAUSE:** {0} only while you control a commander — on the battlefield, not in the zone. Before the loan or the cast, it costs {2}{R}, and it is still the only card in the 99 that answers an ability.

pilot_tips.text: Rent before you buy: a Courser loan gets the attack trigger for five mana and dodges the commander tax entirely — the tax counts casts from the command zone, and a loan is not a cast.

departments.pull_quote: You are not guaranteed a body. You are guaranteed a discount — and it never dies, never taxes, and never taps out.

departments.headline: THE 8.967 PROBLEM
departments.dek: How slow is a nine-mana commander, exactly? We ran the new list 10,000 times on seed 42 and got a number with three decimal places — and one figure that quietly dropped ten points when the deck traded a discount for a combo piece.

callouts.title: THE HEADLINE NUMBER
callouts.text: Commander mean cast turn 8.967, median 9. Cast by turn 6: 0.0% — zero runs in ten thousand. Cast at all by turn 10: 1,366 runs (13.7%). The histogram: 195 casts on turn 7, 104 on turn 8, 618 on turn 9, 449 on turn 10, and 8,634 games where he never left home.

callouts.title: THE PRICE OF THE SWAPS
callouts.text: A cost reducer is drawn by turn 6 in 33.2% of games — down from 43% before the Dragonlord's Servant cut, and the one number the upgrade wave paid for out of pocket. Ramp or fixing overall: 71.6%. The 'turn-5 Ur-Dragon hand' — reducer plus ramp together — assembles by turn 6 in just 23.1% of games. The reducers are the scarce resource; Keep or Ship drills exactly this.

callouts.title: THE LANDS QUIT EARLY
callouts.text: Land drop hit rate: 88.3% on turn 3, 49.7% by turn 6, 35.1% by turn 10. Mean available mana at turn 6 is 4.937, mean bodies 1.463. After turn 4 this deck's mana growth comes from rocks and Treasures, not land drops — which is also why the combo exit runs on Treasures.

callouts.title: THE HANDS ARE FINE
callouts.text: Keep rate on the first seven: 75.1%. Mean mulligans: 0.313. The opening hands are not the problem — the top of the curve is, and hands are judged on whether they bridge to it. A Dragon payoff is drawn by turn 6 in 62.2% of games; payoff plus a castable Dragon by mid-game in only 26.8%.

callouts.title: THE COVER YOU HOLD
callouts.text: A protection or interaction spell is in hand by turn 6 in 66.0% of games. That is the number that authorizes the commit-through-cover playbook — two games in three, the pivot turn can be insured.

captions.Herald's Horn: **MEASURED, NOT MODELED:** the simulator does not model cost reducers — so every commander-lateness figure on this page is the conservative ceiling, and cards like this are why real games run faster.

pilot_tips.text: Weight artifact mana above land count when sequencing: the sim shows land drops decaying to 49.7% by turn 6, so the rock you cast on turn two is still paying on turn nine.

departments.pull_quote: Zero commander casts by turn six in ten thousand games — and the deck got meaner anyway.
departments.note: The stated-assumptions box is non-negotiable and matters doubly here: the model simulates resource development, not games, and it does not model cost reducers, rituals, or extra draw — so the commander figures are honestly pessimistic, which is exactly the direction of error this issue's thesis can afford. Cite every figure exactly as printed; no rounding 8.967 to 9, and the 33.2%-was-43% comparison must name the Servant cut as its cause (strategic_frame key tension), not drift.

departments.headline: COMBATS SIX AND TWELVE
departments.dek: One 7/7 flier, one enchantment, five lands, no help — and a night that ends on combat twelve with twenty-two Treasures in the bank. The checker walked every payment, every untap, and both deaths. Then it did five more files.

callouts.title: THE CONNECTION
callouts.text: Case A-006's scene is deliberately minimal: Old Gnawbone and Aggravated Assault, five untapped lands, two opponents at 40 and 38. Gnawbone connects for 7, and the trigger mints seven Treasures. The question the file settles: can the Dragon fund the whole night alone?

callouts.title: THE LEGAL WALLET
callouts.text: Paying {3}{R}{R} entirely from Treasures is legal — cost payment lets you activate mana abilities, and Treasure's tap-sacrifice is a mana ability that never uses the stack. This matters because five of your mana sources make spells-only mana that can NEVER pay an activated ability. Treasures can. The checker signed it.

callouts.title: NET +2, FOREVER
callouts.text: Each cycle spends five Treasures and mints seven off an unblocked 7/7 — net +2 per combat, no other card required. The engine's real bounds: Gnawbone's survival, a flying or reach blocker, and the supply of opponents. The condition is 5+ combat damage to a player per combat, and Gnawbone's own power clears it standalone.

callouts.title: COMBAT SIX, COMBAT TWELVE
callouts.text: The 40-life opponent dies on combat 6 — seven damage, six connections, 42. The 38-life opponent, holding a groundbound 2/2 that can never block a flier, dies on combat 12. Sequential, not simultaneous: this is a kill-them-in-order engine, and picking the order is your job, not the checker's.

callouts.title: 22 TREASURES, NOT 29
callouts.text: The moment the last opponent's life goes negative, you win immediately — state-based actions end the game before Gnawbone's final trigger ever reaches the stack. You end holding exactly 22 Treasures, not 29. When a verification pipeline counts the Treasures the game never paid out, believe the rest of the ledger.

callouts.title: THE SELF-FUNDING TWIN
callouts.text: Case A-003 is the other flagship: Savage Ventmaw's attack trigger adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G}, the postcombat main pays Assault's {3}{R}{R} with {R} to spare, and the loop runs unbounded at +1 floating mana per cycle. Blockers don't stop the mana — the trigger fires on declaration — but removal, a tap-down, or an attack restriction does.

callouts.title: THE FAIR-SIDE FILES
callouts.text: The bursts that don't need Assault: A-001 rolls a 15 on Ancient Gold Dragon's d20 under Dragon Tempest — fifteen token entries, fifteen triggers reading seventeen Dragons each, up to 255 damage with a priority window between every resolution (and Miirym copies none of them: her trigger says 'nontoken'). A-002 casts one Lathliss under Miirym plus Panharmonicon: two free queens, twelve triggers, 64 damage.

callouts.title: THE HONEST WEAPONS
callouts.text: A-004: your own Blasphemous Act with Wrathful Red Dragon out throws three 13-damage triggers from beyond the grave — 39 at ONE face. Quote it precisely: a one-player execution at 39 or less, never a table-kill, and destroy or exile wraths feed it nothing. A-005: Sneak Attack cheats any Dragon in the 99 into combat for {R} — 17 damage from a Drakuseth that all stands after the mandatory sacrifice — and the same file refutes the commander-cheat reading for good.

captions.Old Gnawbone: **THE PAYMASTER:** Treasures equal to combat damage your creatures deal to players — seven a connection, five an activation, net +2 per combat. Half of the verified table-kill, and the reason the funding question is settled.
captions.Aggravated Assault: **THE SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE:** every infinite in the deck routes through this {3}{R}{R} activation — which is exactly why Deflecting Swat's job is bodyguarding it, and why it comes down the turn it wins.
captions.Savage Ventmaw: **THE SELF-FUNDING TWIN:** six mana on attack that survives the whole turn — one mana more than the reactivation costs. Case A-003 certified the loop; note his mana is spendable on anything, unlike the deck's five spells-only sources.
captions.Wrathful Red Dragon: **THE SWEEPER INVERTER:** damage dealt to your Dragons comes back at any non-Dragon target — even when the Dragons die to the same sweep, via last known information. 39 at one face in case A-004; never call it a table-kill.
captions.Drakuseth, Maw of Flames: **SEVENTEEN FOR ONE:** Sneak Attack's verified exchange rate — 10 trigger damage plus 7 in combat, all of it standing after the end-step sacrifice, because damage is a one-shot effect the sacrifice cannot undo.

pilot_tips.text: Hold Deflecting Swat for the removal spell aimed at Aggravated Assault mid-combo — it is the only card in the 99 that can retarget an ability, and the engine has no second copy of itself.
Land Goldspan Dragon before the Gnawbone turn — his doubling clause makes every Treasure tap for two, so the same connection banks twice the wallet.

departments.pull_quote: Twenty-two Treasures, two dead opponents, and a final trigger the game ended too soon to pay out.
departments.note: The marquee spread of the volume, and the biggest Kill the magazine has run: A-006 gets the numbered sequence at feature scale, A-003 the second feature, then A-001/A-002 as the fair-side movement and A-004/A-005 as the honest-weapons closer. Dossier pointers on all six: 'FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-00N →'. Two discipline rules for the copy: the Cavern-Hoard Dragon + Assault pairing is a CANDIDATE (combo DB, unverified) and appears only with 'needs a stack scenario' language, never beside the verified engines; and A-004's one-player cap plus A-005's refutation are features, not footnotes — the refutation teaser here points to Judge's Desk, where CR 903.6 does the talking. Map-key: ⛃ Treasure · ⚡ mana · ♥ life.

departments.headline: DRAGONS CAN'T BLUFF
departments.dek: The table sees five-colour Dragons and prices in a turn-eight haymaker — while the actual clock is a five-mana enchantment they've been taught to answer on sight. How do you keep three opponents wrong about which deck you are?

callouts.title: YOUR COVER STORY IS TRUE
callouts.text: For four turns you genuinely are the slow deck: 4.937 mana and 1.463 bodies at turn 6, commander cast by then in 0.0% of runs. Nobody watching for The Ur-Dragon is watching the actual clock. Ramp, fix, deploy a modal 3-drop, and let the table's read stay comfortable — it is doing your deflection for you.

callouts.title: THE THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: The exact board state that flips you to archenemy: Aggravated Assault on the battlefield with funding visible — Treasures banked, or a Ventmaw pointed at someone. Bracket-4 tables answer Assault on sight, so it does not come down early as a value drop. It comes down inside the turn it wins, after the table's interaction has been counted, with Deflecting Swat held for the removal spell you know is coming.

callouts.title: THE TELL LADDER
callouts.text: What the table answers, in order: Aggravated Assault on sight; Miirym, because everyone has felt the Panharmonicon doubling; Sneak Attack, because {R} for a Drakuseth is a rate nobody forgives; then Dragon Tempest once your board is wide. Sequence the scariest piece last — every tell you show early is a rotation of removal aimed at the engine before it runs.

callouts.title: THE DETERRENT SEAT
callouts.text: Wrathful Red Dragon changes the pod's sweeper calculus while just standing there: any damage-based wrath now hands you 13 per Dragon to throw at one face (case A-004 — a one-player execution, and say so at the table; honesty is also deterrence). Embrace archenemy status in exactly two spots: the Assault window, and any turn a damage sweeper is likely with Wrathful out. Every other turn, stay small.

captions.Tiamat: **THE PUBLIC COUNTDOWN:** five differently named Dragons to hand, in full view — the loudest signal this deck can send, and the moment three players start doing wrath math.
captions.Sneak Attack: **THE RATE NOBODY FORGIVES:** the table knows what one red mana means once this resolves — which is why it resolves the turn it matters, not the turn you draw it.

pilot_tips.text: Welcome the wrath you cannot stop — in the pilot's token-heavy pods, Bidding's symmetry returns your graveyard full of Dragons and their tokens return nothing, because tokens never hit the graveyard as cards.

departments.pull_quote: You are never scarier than in the turns you are weakest — your whole political job is keeping the table's clock wrong about yours.

departments.headline: JAM, BAIT, OR WAIT?
departments.dek: One board asks whether nine mana of commander goes into five untapped Azorius lands; the other hands you a Tiamat trigger with a telegraphed board wipe across the table. Commit to your line out loud — then read ours.

callouts.title: SPREAD ONE — TURN 7
callouts.text: Urza's Incubator and Dragon's Hoard down, seven lands, The Ur-Dragon castable for seven with Heroic Intervention in hand — and the control player has five untapped lands and two counters already spent this game. Three branches: jam with backup, bait with a three-mana Miirym, or hold everything and play the Forest.

callouts.title: SPREAD TWO — TURN 8
callouts.text: Tiamat just resolved and her search trigger is on the stack: up to five differently named Dragon cards, your pile to design — into seven lands of Supreme-Verdict-shaped mana. Which five names, and in what order do they hit the table? The pile IS the decision, and one tempting v3 fetch is a named trap.

captions.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: **THE THREE-MANA QUESTION:** with Incubator and Eminence she costs {G}{U}{R} — the cheapest possible probe of a counter-heavy hand, and ward {2} taxes the answer either way.
captions.Heroic Intervention: **READ THE FINE PRINT:** hexproof and indestructible are shields for permanents you control. Your commander on the stack is a spell — this card has never once countered a Counterspell.

pilot_tips.text: Never hold Heroic Intervention as counterspell insurance — it protects permanents on the battlefield, and a commander on the stack is not yet one of them.

departments.pull_quote: Spend your one realistic cast when it is most likely to stick — and sequence the scariest piece last.
departments.note: Two spreads from decisions/001 and 002, both re-authored for the v3 list. The recommendation is revealed only after all branches, per the department's hard rule — neither headline nor dek may telegraph it. Spread one's coaching carries two gems: protection cannot save a spell on the stack, and the card that actually defends the window — Deflecting Swat, free with a commander spell on the stack — is in the LIST but not in this HAND, which is itself the lesson. Spread two's wrath-math masterclass includes the named refusal: Wrathful Red Dragon is NOT sweeper insurance against Verdict-shaped mana, because destroy effects deal no damage and feed him nothing (the A-004 boundary, applied). Branch citations (702.11b, 903.8, 903.9a) render with their ✓ treatment inside otherwise ★ spreads, exactly as the artifacts carry them.

departments.headline: WHO BEATS THE HOARD
departments.dek: Dedicated combo owns your clock, sweeper control walks into a verified trap, and the aggro seat was never your problem. Know which chair at the pod is actually dangerous — and which of your outs is legal fuel.

threats.read: The seat that beats you: their inevitability is faster than your mean-turn-8.967 commander and cheaper than your engines. Answer economy is everything — the last profitable moment for a held counter is their win attempt, never a value spell. Post-swap you also race credibly: your own two-card lines assemble at MV 6 or less, so the frame is dueling pivot windows, not pure reaction. The pilot's pods skew white-less and counter-light, so plan for stack fights, not Silence effects.

Your defining matchup, now with a verified inversion clause. Wave deployment costs you little — your mean board is 1.463 bodies at turn 6 anyway — and your rebuild is structurally cheap: the enchantment layer (Assault, Sneak Attack, Temur Ascendancy, Garruk's Uprising) survives creature wraths, Atsushi dies forward into three unrestricted Treasures, eminence discounts every recast, and Patriarch's Bidding turns their reset into your best turn. With Wrathful Red Dragon out, every DAMAGE sweeper is a trap for them — 39 at one face (case A-004). Know the boundary: destroy-all and exile-all wraths feed him nothing.

The lock forces you into the beatdown seat, racing its completion. Taxes hit your 5-to-7 shelf hard, but three things break the math: eminence accrues from the command zone where permanent-hate cannot reach, Treasure bursts pay taxes in lump sums, and the Assault engines need exactly one clean combat — the Ventmaw loop is self-funding at +1 mana per cycle (case A-003), so a single resolved activation goes over any incremental lock. Aim your sparse removal at whatever stops combats or taxes activations — Assault is the whole exit.

You are the control seat: roughly 120 combined life stands behind three defenses, their math is worst at this table, and your fliers blank ground boards. Trade time, not cards — Crux of Fate destroys every non-Dragon and keeps your entire hoard, and Blasphemous Act with Wrathful out is a kill on the aggro player, not just a reset. Their clock runs out of gas exactly when yours starts.

pilot_tips.text: Against creature decks, cast Crux of Fate on the mode that keeps your board — destroy all non-Dragons and attack into the wreckage.
Hold Dovin's Veto for the counter-war itself — it is the only answer you own that cannot be answered back.

departments.pull_quote: Nine answers in sixty-six spells. Spend them on the spell that ends the game — never on the one that merely looks scary.

departments.headline: ENGINES, WALLETS, DRAGONS
departments.dek: Ninety-nine cards doing six jobs: run the verified engines, fund them legally, pay off every Dragon, cheapen the next one, insure the big turn, and — in exactly nine slots — answer everyone else. Rank matters, and the case-file cards lead.

roster.role: The discount stack — the other commander
The velocity crew — draw on permanents, on purpose
Interaction — all nine slots of it

captions.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: **SPELLS ONLY, AND WE MEAN ONLY:** this mana casts Dragon creature spells and nothing else — an activated ability is not a spell, so it cannot pay Aggravated Assault, or even Haven's own recursion mode. Five of your sources carry this restriction; count your unrestricted mana separately.
captions.Atsushi, the Blazing Sky: **DIES FORWARD:** three unrestricted Treasures on death — the legal wallet case A-006 certified. He holds the slot Sarkhan, Fireblood lost for making exactly the mana that couldn't pay the win.
captions.Enlightened Tutor: **THE ASSEMBLY SPELL:** one mana for any artifact or enchantment on top — Aggravated Assault above all, because the combo exit is an enchantment. The cheapest way to put a case file on schedule.
captions.Patriarch's Bidding: **THE REBUILD:** every Dragon in your graveyard returns at once, re-firing Tempest, Valkas, Terror, and Miirym on the way in. Mind the {B}{B} — black is the deck's thinnest colour, 11 land sources against a 36-source target.

pilot_tips.text: Pay Dragon's Hoard's draw activation with lands and rocks — none of the five spells-only sources can ever activate an ability, no matter how much Dragon mana is floating.

departments.note: Grouped by role, ranked by load: the nine case-file cards open the page at feature scale — every one of them appears in a checker-passed artifact — and the three-card wallet group is the issue's honest tension rendered as layout. The interaction group's header does the teaching: nine answers is the linear-deck tradeoff, stated, not hidden. With the sideboard retired, the roster is the whole collection — twelve groups, the full 100, no bench strip; a reader hunting for more cards gets pointed to Upgrade Watch's Lookout, not to a box that no longer exists. deck-facts caveat for the copy: 14 maindeck cards have no role-taxonomy entry (Assault, Sneak Attack, Deflecting Swat, and Panharmonicon among them), so every role count this page prints is a floor, not an exact number.

departments.headline: SEVENTY-SIX HANDS
departments.dek: Who painted your deck? Seventy-six different people across forty-one sets — the count leader stops at four cards, and the artist we feature earned it by subject, not volume: he painted the commander this whole issue argues about.

featured.note: Let's be honest about the ranking first, because this department reads the table instead of quoting it: the count leader is Adam Paquette at four entries, with Grzegorz Rutkowski, Joshua Raphael, and Jaime Jones at three — and the analysis itself says no standout, because four cards is a cluster, not a signature, in a 95-entry pool where 76 artists appear. So the feature is an editorial choice, made openly: Jaime Jones painted three cards, and they happen to be the issue's spine — The Ur-Dragon himself, the commander on the cover; Temur Ascendancy, the haste-plus-draw enchantment the pivot window runs on; and Dragonlord Kolaghan, the haste anthem that opens that window all by herself. Three cards, all load-bearing. Nobody curated this concentration — the analysis flags no collector-number runs — it is simply where the pilot's printings landed, and that is the story: a deck assembled from forty-one sets, whose three most thesis-critical cards came from one hand anyway. Counting discipline, printed every issue: we count cards, never copies — Jonas De Ro's Mountain appears four times and Tomáš Honz's Forest three, and each is one entry, because a spare basic is a printing fact, not a second painting.
featured.hero_caption: **THE COMMANDER'S PORTRAIT:** Jaime Jones's Ur-Dragon — the card this issue spends thirty pages arguing you should almost never cast, painted like the reason you will anyway.

also_worth_noting.note: Four entries, the count lead: Blood Crypt, Cinder Glade, Steam Vents, plus Dragon's Hoard. Three of the four are the mana — the manabase-painter of the collection, and the honest count-led alternative to our pick.
Three entries: Drakuseth, Maw of Flames, Urza's Incubator, and Rootbound Crag — the haymaker, the discount, and a land that casts them both.
Three entries spread across three departments of the deck: Terror of the Peaks in the payoff layer, Rivaz of the Claw in the discount stack, Heroic Intervention at the insurance desk.

captions.Dragonlord Kolaghan: **THE THIRD JONES:** a haste anthem on a 6/5 flier — the painting that opens the pivot window, from the same hand as the commander himself.
captions.Temur Ascendancy: **THE SECOND JONES:** haste plus a card per big Dragon entering — the quiet enchantment this issue's strategy pages cite more than any creature.

departments.pull_quote: No artist owns this deck. Seventy-six hands built the hoard — and we count the cards, not the copies.
departments.note: Renderer recomputes all counts from artist-credits, which now covers the 100 and nothing else — the retired sideboard is out of the pool, so every figure on this page shrank honestly: 95 entries, 100 copies, 76 artists. Art File fast-facts: 41 sets, top sets Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander (8 entries), Lorwyn Eclipsed Commander (7), and Tarkir: Dragonstorm (7); treatments — 13 legendary frames, 8 enchantment frames, 1 foil (the foil gets its sheen, a property of the physical card), 0 borderless. drop_runs is empty, so no bought-whole caveat is needed. If the orchestrator prefers a count-led feature, Adam Paquette (4 entries, all in the 100) is the honest alternative; Jones's three are unchanged by the retirement, which is part of why the subject-matter feature still holds.

departments.headline: MULLIGAN FOR FUNCTION
departments.dek: The sim keeps 75.1% of first sevens, so most hands are fine — the drill is spotting which of these four is the trap. Rule on each before you read the verdict, and remember: the commander is the one card you never mulligan toward.

hands.why: Three lands, ramp, an early payoff — and a cost reducer, the acceleration that matters most. A reducer is drawn by turn 6 in only 33.2% of games; when you are dealt one, you do not ship it hunting prettier Dragons.

Five lands and two haymakers is the classic trap seven: nothing to do until turn five, no reducer, no payoff, no protection. Lands plus seven-drops with no bridge is the named ship in this deck's mulligan rule.

Three lands, Sol Ring, held protection, and half of case A-003 — an easy keep. The drill is the sequencing: Aggravated Assault in the opener is a HOLD, not a keep-reason. It is the deck's loudest tell and it wins nothing before a board and funding exist; casting it on turn three is donating a removal target.

hands.verdict: SHIP — the colours can't cast it
hands.why: Three lands, zero blue or black sources — and this hand is blue-and-black shaped. Five colours is a real tax: black has just 11 land sources against Bidding's {B}{B}, and a hand whose colours cannot cast its spells is a mulligan no matter how good the spells are.

captions.Urza's Incubator: **THE KEEP SIGNAL:** a hand with a cost reducer is a keep almost regardless of what else it holds — the reducers, not the land drops, compress a nine-drop curve into a castable one.

pilot_tips.text: Count a protection spell as a keep-bonus, not a dead card — held cover is what authorizes the wave turn, and it is in hand by turn 6 in 66.0% of games.

departments.pull_quote: You never mulligan for the commander — Eminence works from the command zone, so a hand that casts him is worth nothing extra.

departments.headline: THE SHOPPING HOARD
departments.dek: The six swaps are closed history and the bench is retired — so this Upgrade Watch goes shopping instead. On the Lookout: ten ranked picks scouted from the whole card pool, three evidence channels, and one headline want — a second copy of the engine every infinite in this deck routes through.

callouts.title: THE SCOUT'S METHOD
callouts.text: On the Lookout is a validated, ranked top-10 read of the card pool through three evidence channels: the obsolescence index, the combo lines a candidate would open with cards already in the 99, and the synergy graph. The evidence lines are data — traced, ranked, checkable. The picks are judgment, and wear the ★ to say so. And every combo line a pick would open is a candidate that needs its own stack scenario before anyone leans a game on it; the report says so pick by pick, and so do we.

callouts.title: THE REDUNDANCY BLOCK
callouts.text: The frame's single-Assault dependency is the theme most of the ten answer. Hellkite Charger is the literal second Assault — an extra-combat engine on a Dragon body, so Eminence discounts it, Sarkhan's Triumph tutors it, and all five spells-only sources can cast it (its {5}{R}{R} activation, like Assault's, they still cannot pay — Treasures fund it exactly as case A-006 verified). The Reaver Cleaver is a three-mana Old Gnawbone for whoever carries it, pairing directly with the Assault already sleeved — the most popular line any candidate opens. Ancient Copper Dragon is a second Gnawbone with dice: d20 Treasures per connection, mean 10.5, minimum 1 — 'near-infinite' in the record, because the roll can undershoot the five mana Assault needs.

callouts.title: THE UNTAP WALLET
callouts.text: Two picks fund Assault with the one mana nothing in this deck restricts: lands. Sword of Feast and Famine untaps them all on combat damage — the next {3}{R}{R} is covered before your postcombat main — while stripping a card from the defender and shielding the carrier from black and green removal. Bear Umbra untaps on attack, before blockers, so it pays out even when the attacker is chumped, and umbra armor eats the first removal spell aimed at the engine's carrier. Neither line is verified; both mirror the funding architecture cases A-003 and A-006 already proved.

callouts.title: THE OFF-ASSAULT AXIS
callouts.text: Helm of the Host is the one candidate whose infinite skips Assault entirely: it pairs with the Scourge of the Throne already in the 99 — each nonlegendary copy's dethrone grants another combat, IF the attack-the-most-life condition holds every iteration, which is exactly what its scenario must settle — and off-combo it stamps a fresh nonlegendary Miirym, Terror, or Gnawbone each combat, scaling every verified trigger stack. Selvala, Heart of the Wilds turns your biggest Dragon's power into unrestricted any-colour mana and untaps with every Assault activation; Neheb, the Eternal converts the damage your combats already deal into postcombat red mana that legally pays the next one.

callouts.title: THE TWO CONSISTENCY PICKS
callouts.text: Three Visits is the Lookout's one obsolescence-traced entry: similarity 0.9983 to Skyshroud Claim at lower cost, fetching any of the deck's seven Forest-typed duals untapped two turns earlier — functional copies three and four of the Nature's Lore effect the 71.6% ramp-by-turn-6 figure leans on, with the Claim as the artifact's named natural cut. Ancient Silver Dragon is the pilot's own requisition against the role budget's biggest hole (draw, six cards short): d20 cards per connection, no maximum hand size — and its delivery is the one already-verified thing on this page, because case A-005 proved Sneak Attack cheats any Dragon in the 99 into combat for {R}.

callouts.title: THE HONESTY CLAUSE
callouts.text: What the scout refuses to sell: Ad Nauseam is the pool's only Game Changer candidate, and it sits excluded on fit, not floor — this deck's mana values make the life cost brutal, and the floor is already 4 by the pilot's own request. The synergy channel produced only noise for this deck, so no pick carries a synergy claim — we print the empty channel rather than pad it. And the two cards the pilot named in feedback, Hellkite Tyrant and Faeburrow Elder, appear in no evidence channel at all; carrying either is a pilot's call the data cannot back, and we say that plainly rather than pretend the scout found them.

captions.Skyshroud Claim: **THE TRACED CUT:** the obsolescence index lists Three Visits as its strict upgrade — similarity 0.9983, lower cost, the same Forest-typed duals arriving untapped two turns earlier. The one Lookout entry with a full paper trail, and the one named cut in the 100.
captions.Cavern-Hoard Dragon: **THE SLOT UNDER REVIEW:** his Treasure count depends on the defender's artifacts; Ancient Copper Dragon's depends on a d20 you roll yourself. If the redundancy picks land, this is the slot they price against — and the third contained infinite leaves with him, so the artifact marks the cut ★ judgment, not data.
captions.Sneak Attack: **THE VERIFIED DELIVERY:** case A-005 already proved this cheats any Dragon in the 99 into combat for {R} — which is exactly how an eight-mana d20 draw engine like Ancient Silver Dragon would want to arrive.

pilot_tips.text: Treat Aggravated Assault as irreplaceable until a redundancy pick clears its stack scenario — it is the only extra-combat engine in the 100, and every contained infinite routes through it.

departments.pull_quote: One removal spell still turns off every infinite at once. The scout's report is the fix — priced, ranked, and honestly unverified.
departments.note: The renderer draws the On the Lookout section from upgrade_watch.json (validated, ranked top-10 against decklist edc6644d0683); sideboard_analysis.json no longer exists and nothing may reference it. Tier-costume integrity: the department badge stays ◆; the evidence lines (obsolescence trace, opened combo lines, EDHREC ranks, role shortfalls) are ◆ validator-traced; every pick rationale is ★ and the artifact marks each one so — never restyle a pick as data, and never let an opened line near verified costume: all of them carry 'needs a stack scenario', including the three the gaps rank worth buying first. The swap paper trail (six swaps, two waves, floor 3 to 4) now lives in manual_prose.json's upgrades intro and HISTORY.md's four lines — this spread references that story in one breath and then shops; it does not re-tell it. The artifact's two natural cuts (Skyshroud Claim, Cavern-Hoard Dragon) print as the scout's own ★ suggestions, never as decisions already made.

departments.headline: SIX FILES, NO ASTERISKS
departments.dek: Every claim in this issue traces to one of six case files — two infinites, two bursts, one inversion quoted with its cap, and one file that refutes its own headline and names the card that does the job instead.
departments.note: Renderer-generated from the checker-passed artifacts; nothing summarized, truncated, or paraphrased — every citation verbatim in typewriter face against the June 19, 2026 rules. CASE A-001 (Dragon Tempest + Ancient Gold Dragon burst; pass, 2 iterations): 15 tokens, 17-per-trigger, up to 255, with the Miirym-copies-nothing finding. CASE A-002 (Miirym under Panharmonicon; pass, 2 iterations): two free queens, 64 damage across twelve triggers, and the finite-loop proof. CASE A-003 (Savage Ventmaw + Aggravated Assault; pass, 2 iterations): the flagship infinite, +1 mana per cycle, with the spells-only funding rule stated. CASE A-004 (Wrathful Red Dragon + Blasphemous Act; pass, 2 iterations): three LKI triggers, 39 at one face, SBAs before targeting — the file's own answer opens 'Not a table-kill', and the manila prints that line at full size. CASE A-005 (Sneak Attack; pass, 2 iterations): the verified 99-cheater and the REFUTED commander cheat, CR 903.6 verbatim, Hellkite Courser named — run the refutation as the department's centerpiece stamp, per the house style of celebrating the no. CASE A-006 (Old Gnawbone + Aggravated Assault; pass, 2 iterations): Treasure funding legal, net +2, deaths on combats 6 and 12, and the 22-not-29 ending where the game's own conclusion outruns the last trigger.

NEXT ISSUE: 'TO BE ANNOUNCED' per issue.json — run as authored, do not invent a deck; tease the mystery straight ('Vol. 006 is classified until the decklist clears the checker'). Colophon: rules version 2026-06-19, decklist sha256 edc6644d0683…, goldfish seed 42 / 10,000 iterations, bracket floor 4 (computed), generation provenance, Fan Content Policy line. Close the loop with the version story: this issue was updated in place, and HISTORY.md now runs four lines — an import, two swap waves (six swaps, floor 3 to 4), and a sideboard retired at the pilot's request, its full record standing in git history — plus one line reminding the reader the whole claim ledger is six case files and a simulator, both in the back of the book.

rhythm_notes: Canonical order alternates cleanly. By the Numbers (dense analysis, five figure callouts) hands off to The Kill, which is the heaviest technical content in any issue to date but reads as narrative — six files are staged as three movements (the Assault engines, the fair-side bursts, the honest weapons) so the peak builds rather than plateaus, with full sequences deferred to Judge's Desk. Politics Table (reflection) cools the reader before the participation spike of What's Your Play?; Know Your Enemy (reference, dense) is followed by the browsing-mode 99 and then Featured Artist, the issue's long exhale after three straight strategy departments. Keep or Ship re-engages with practice before Upgrade Watch — now the pool-scout spread, pure imagination-mode shopping with a hard honesty clause, a story rather than a spec sheet — gliding into the opt-in depth of Judge's Desk. No two dense departments sit adjacent. Pun ledger: EMINENCE DOMAIN and THE SHOPPING HOARD in headlines, 'dies forward' as recurring furniture wit — three spent, under the four-pun ceiling.
gaps: Cavern-Hoard Dragon + Aggravated Assault is the only maindeck-contained Assault line without a stack artifact — a scenario would settle whether its defender-artifact-count funding sustains in the pilot's Treasure-heavy pods. Until then the issue names it a candidate everywhere it appears — doubly relevant now that the Lookout marks his slot as Ancient Copper Dragon's natural cut.

The Lookout's highest-value stack scenarios to buy, in the artifact's own order: The Reaver Cleaver + Aggravated Assault (Treasure accounting mirroring A-006), Old Gnawbone + Hellkite Charger, and Helm of the Host + Scourge of the Throne — the last shares the open dethrone question below, and its answer decides whether the loop is real.

Two frame candidates need scenarios before anyone claims them: Sneak Attack at instant speed in response to a damage sweeper (extending A-004 into a reactive ambush), and whether a Miirym token copy survives Sneak Attack's end-step sacrifice — the latter also has to resolve the legend rule on legendary cheat targets.

Scourge of the Throne's dethrone recheck on the second combat remains an open rules question (card_roles flags it) — currently coached as 'plan the first combat to be the one that counts', and now also the gating question for the Lookout's Helm of the Host line.

Strategy DB gaps inherited from the frame: extra-combat chaining as a school, kill-order sequencing when a line kills sequentially (A-006 does exactly this), cheat-into-play economics, and typal payoff density — four research-pass topics this issue works around with the nearest existing frames.
next_issue is 'TO BE ANNOUNCED' in issue.json — the back page runs it straight, but the orchestrator should confirm before print whether Vol. 006 has a name.

Featured Artist has no computed standout in the post-retirement pool (95 entries, 76 artists; lead cluster Adam Paquette at 4 cards) — the plan authors Jaime Jones on subject-matter grounds (3 entries, all thesis cards, unchanged by the sideboard retirement) and says so openly. Count-led alternative: Adam Paquette, 4 entries, all in the 100.

14 maindeck cards have no card_roles.json entry (Aggravated Assault, Sneak Attack, Deflecting Swat, Panharmonicon among them), so every role count the issue prints is a floor, not an exact count — the 99 department note carries this caveat for the renderer.

Whether the Dragonlord's Servant cut's reducer drop (43% to 33.2% by t6) matters in practice is unmeasurable from goldfish alone — and with the bench retired there is no standing return case: reacquiring a reducer is now a pool decision, and no reducer appears in any Lookout evidence channel. By the Numbers prints the comparison with its cause named.

The Wrathful Red Dragon inversion depends on the opposing meta running damage-based sweepers; in a pod that wraths with destroy/exile effects only, A-004's deterrence value drops to zero — Know Your Enemy states the boundary, and the coaching should resist overselling the trump in white-less pods where Farewell-style exile wraths are common.

Ad Nauseam is the pool's only Game Changer candidate (Ad Nauseam + Teferi's Protection, infinite draw, unverified), excluded from the Lookout on fit, not floor — the pilot approved bracket 4, so if the orchestrator wants it re-litigated the floor is not the objection.

Pilot feedback names Hellkite Tyrant and Faeburrow Elder; neither appears in any Lookout evidence channel (no obsolescence entry, no combo line with the 99, no qualifying synergy shortlist, no shorted role — ramp is over budget at 13/10). Carrying them anyway is an orchestrator/pilot decision the data cannot back; the Honesty Clause callout prints this rather than hiding it.

Role-budget shorts in lands (-7), sweeper (-2), and recursion (-2) have no evidenced pool candidate in any channel; the lands figure is the builder's 36-land prior against this deck's deliberate 29 and likely needs the pilot's judgment, not a pick.

The synergy evidence channel produced only noise for this deck (format-wide shortlists, Ramp + Cost Reduction pairings) — no Lookout pick carries a synergy_partners_in_deck claim, and the copy must not imply the graph endorsed any pick.
